titleStmt.title: A Probabilistic Scheduling Framework for Mixed-Criticality Systems

analytic.title: A Probabilistic Scheduling Framework for Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We propose a probabilistic scheduling framework for the design and development of mixed-criticality systems, i.e., where tasks with different levels of criticality need to be scheduled on a shared resource. Whereas highly critical tasks normally require hard real-time guarantees, less or non•critical ones may be degraded or even temporarily discarded at runtime. We hence propose giving probabilistic (instead of deterministic) real-time guarantees on lowcriticality tasks. This simplifies the analysis and reduces conservativeness on the one hand. On the other hand, probabilistic guarantees can be tuned by the designer to reach a desired level of assurance. We illustrate these and other benefits of our framework based on extensive simulations.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: In diHerent industrial domains such as automotive systems and avionics, there is a trend to consolidate software functions onto fewer processing units with the aim of reducing complexity and costs. Applications with different levels of criticality -originally running in isolation -now start sharing processors. As a. result, since critical tasks should never be affected by non-critical ones, there is a need for techniques that allow designing and developing such mixedcriticality (MC) systems while still guaranteeing safety.

One of the major challenges with MC systems is to verify a correct timing behavior. Particularly, in practice, highcriticality (HI) tasks may tempomrily increase their execution demands at runtime in response to some event [19].

Clearly, if we find an upper bound on this increase, we can ta.lre provisions for the worst case. However, this leads to an inefficient design, since the system will be underutilized most of the time.

As a consequence, to improve design efficiency, a number of scheduling techniques have appeared in the embedded and real-time systems literature. These techniques introduce operation modes at different levels of criticality L and exploit the fact that not all tasks require the same degree of assurance at a given such L. Hence, rather than taking worst-case provisions, these techniques either degrade or even discard low-criticality (LO) tasks to account for a transitory increase in HI execution demand [4,2,13].

Contributions. In this paper, we consider a fixed-priority scheduling and, in line with the above-mentioned techniques, propose degrading LO tasks to accommodate an increase in HI execution demand at a given L. While still providing deterministic timing guarantees for HI tasks, in contrast to other approaches from the literature, we derive probabilistic such guarantees for LO tasks instead. To this end, we propose randomizing LO tasks in a controlled manner.

More specifically, the jobs of any LO task Ts are arti.fici.ally delayed upon release by an amount of time that is randomly selected from [0, Ti -Di] being Di ::5 n. Here Ti denotes T.'S minimum separation between any two jobs, whereas D, denotes its relative deadline. Based on this, we can compute the probability p that a job of T, misses its deadline at the critical instant. As discussed later, p is constant and independent of the individual jobs.

We further define a probabilistic timing guarantee on any Ti by a 4-tuple r. = (I', k, n, 6). Pis a desired upper bound on the probability P that k (or more) out of n consecutive T.'S jobs miss their deadlines by more than 6 . Do time, where 6 is defined as Ti'S tolerable tardiness in mode L. Since p is independent of the individual T.'S jobs, P can be computed using the well-known binomial distribution. Note that similar timing guarantees (i.e., number of successes out of number of trials) have been proposed before in the context of stream processing applications [12].

In contrast to other approaches from the literature, the proposed approach of this paper can be adapted so as not to require monitoring HI tasks' execution time at runtime. In addition, it allows reducing the amount of conservativeness as illustrated later by extensive experiments.

Structure of the paper. We first discuss related work in Section 2. Section 3 introduces our models and assumptions, whereas Section 4 is concerned with schedulability analysis for MC systems under fixed priorities. The proposed technique is introduced in Section 5. Section 6 presents experimental results and Section 7 concludes the paper.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: In this section, we briefly revise the rich literature concerning MC systems -a complete overview can be found in [9]. The problematic around MC systems was first addressed by Vestal in [19]. In particular, Vestal showed that the wellknown deadline monotonic (DM) policy is not optimal for MC systems, where HI tasks may temporarily increase their execution demands. Since then, different approaches have been proposed for MC systems under both fixed and dynamic priorities.

For single processors, Baruah et al. analyzed different priority assignments and the resulting response times under fixed priorities [4]. In [5], Baruah et al. presented a further priority assignment with a partially better performance than those in [4]. Burns and Davis proposed another fixedpriority scheme where non-preemptive regions are added to tasks and showed that this leads to a even better performance than previously published schemes [8].

Under EDF, in [3], Baruah et al. proposed the EDF-VD algorithm to schedule a mix of HI and LO tasks. EDF-VD introduces two operation modes and uses a prioritypromotion scheme by uniformly scaling deadlines of HI tasks. A speed-up factor for EDF-VD was first obtained in [3] as (V5+ 1)/2. Later this speed-up factor was improved to 4/3 [2]. A more flexible approach with per-task deadline scaling was presented by Ekberg and Yi [10] [11]. Ekberg and Yi characterized the execution demand of MC systems under EDF by deriving demand bound functions for the LO and the HI mode.

Improvements to the original EDF -VD have also been proposed. In [18], Su and Zhu used an elastic task model [15] to improve resource utilization in MC systems. In [21], Zhao et al. applied preemption thresholds [20] to MC scheduling in order to better utilize the processing unit. Recently, Huang et al. proposed speeding up processors to account for increases in HI execution demand when switching to HI mode [14]. Huang et al. made use of Ekberg and Yi's demand bound functions to compute the necessary speed-up factors that guarantee meeting a.ll deadlines.

For multiprocessors, a partitioned and a global scheduling approach both based on EDF-VD were proposed in [6]. According to this work, partitioned behaves better than global scheduling in the context of MC systems. Further, in [16], Pathan studies global MC scheduling under fixed priorities and gives a schedulability test based on response time analysis for more than two criticality levels.

Whereas, in the above approaches, LO tasks are discarded to accommodate an increase in HI execution demand, Huang et al. rather proposed degrading LO tasks [13], for which they derive degraded timing guarantees. Recently, Ren and Phan proposed task grouping and a server-based approach to provide guarantees to both HI and LO tlU!lks on multiprocessors [17]. This paper follows this line of work. Similar to [13] and [17], we propose not discarding LO tasks in case HI execution demand increases, but rather degrading them. However, as already mentioned, we derive probabilistic instead of deterministic timing guarantees for degraded LO tasks.

div.p: In this section we introduce our proposed probabilistic framework for MC systems. As mentioned above, this is based on randomizing LO tasks To at a given L so as to allow for a probabilistic analysis. In particular, our approach is based on the following two principles:

(i) The release times of all Ti'S jobs in mode L > Li are artificially delayed by a random ~i -we omit an index identifying individual jobs to simplify notation -that is uniformly chosen from [0, Ti -D.].

div.head: CONCLUDING REMARKS
div.p: In this paper, we studied the problem of mixed-criticality scheduling under fixed priorities, i.e., where a mix of tasks with different levels of criticality share the processor. In particular, based on a controlled randomization, we derived probabilistic (instead of deterministic) timing guarantees for LO tasks, which allows considerably reducing the amount of pessimism in the design and development of such systems. In contrast to other approaches from the literature, the proposed technique has the additional advantage tha.t it can be modified 80 as not to require runtime monitoring. Finally, we presented a number of experiments based on synthetic data to illustrate the utility and better performance of the proposed technique.
